title: Finding One Band in a Smear
endLine: Gels sort DNA and RNA by size; probes reveal sequence identity.

scenes.tts: How do you find one gene when its DNA fragment hides in a smear? Cut genomic DNA with a restriction enzyme, a sequence-specific cutter, and a gel shows a crowded blur. To spot one, you need both its size and its identity.
scenes.caption: How do you find one gene when its DNA fragment hides in a smear? Cut genomic DNA with a restriction enzyme, a sequence-specific cutter, and a gel shows a crowded blur. To spot one, you need both its size and its identity.
scenes.visual: Schematic vertical agarose gel slab filling at least 60% of frame height. A single sample lane drifts downward into a dense glowing smear of many DNA fragments. One hidden target band pulses faintly inside the blur beside a high-contrast question mark; at most 4 elements on screen.
scenes.narration: How do you find one gene when its DNA fragment hides in a smear? Cut genomic DNA with a restriction enzyme, a sequence-specific cutter, and a gel shows a crowded blur. To spot one, you need both its size and its identity.

scenes.visual: The schematic gel smear dims slightly while slow ambient fragments drift gently; the title 'Finding One Band in a Smear' appears cleanly in high-contrast text above the slab.

scenes.tts: First, load the cut DNA into an agarose gel. Its negatively charged backbone moves toward the positive electrode. Smaller fragments travel faster through the mesh. A size ladder in a neighboring lane turns position into length. Still, a right-sized band shows size, not identity.
scenes.caption: First, load the cut DNA into an agarose gel. Its negatively charged backbone moves toward the positive electrode. Smaller fragments travel faster through the mesh. A size ladder in a neighboring lane turns position into length. Still, a right-sized band shows size, not identity.
scenes.visual: Same schematic gel slab, now with minus at top and plus at bottom. Before narration names them, cut DNA bands enter the top wells and migrate downward: shorter schematic bars move ahead of longer ones through a subtle mesh. In the left lane, a schematic size ladder resolves into evenly spaced reference rungs; a highlight brackets one band with 'Size only'.
scenes.narration: First, load the cut DNA into an agarose gel. Its negatively charged backbone moves toward the positive electrode. Smaller fragments travel faster through the mesh. A size ladder in a neighboring lane turns position into length. Still, a right-sized band shows size, not identity.

scenes.tts: In 1975, Edwin Southern added identity without losing the gel's separation. DNA in the gel is denatured into single strands so a probe can pair. Capillary flow transfers that exact pattern onto a cellulose nitrate membrane. A labeled probe washes across, sticking only to matching, complementary sequences. The gel sorts by size; pairing with the probe, hybridization, reveals identity.

scenes.visual: Carried gel slab transforms in place (schematic, no molecular structures). Paired schematic lines inside the gel unzip into single strands. A rising liquid front carries the exact lane pattern upward onto a flat cellulose nitrate membrane laid atop the gel. Drifting glowing probe strands sweep across the membrane, lock onto one complementary band, wash away elsewhere, and leave only that crisp band lit on film.

scenes.tts: In 1977, James Alwine, David Kemp and George Stark adapted transfer for RNA. Its name, Northern blot, began as a joke on Southern's name. RNA separates by size, transfers to a membrane, and binds a labeled DNA probe. Band intensity reports how much messenger RNA of that gene the cells contain.
scenes.caption: In 1977, James Alwine, David Kemp and George Stark adapted transfer for RNA. Its name, Northern blot, began as a joke on Southern's name. RNA separates by size, transfers to a membrane, and binds a labeled DNA probe. Band intensity reports how much messenger RNA of that gene the cells contain.
scenes.visual: Same schematic gel-to-membrane layout switches label from 'Southern: DNA' to 'Northern: RNA' with a small compass cue. Single-stranded schematic RNA fragments separate by size, transfer onto the membrane, and meet drifting labeled DNA probes. Two adjacent sample lanes light up at the same height, one faint and one bright, showing schematic band intensity.
scenes.narration: In 1977, James Alwine, David Kemp and George Stark adapted transfer for RNA. Its name, Northern blot, began as a joke on Southern's name. RNA separates by size, transfers to a membrane, and binds a labeled DNA probe. Band intensity reports how much messenger RNA of that gene the cells contain.

scenes.tts: Test this on a chromosome's two copies. Suppose an enzyme cuts one copy's version, or allele, into a long piece, and the other's into a short piece. Normal tissue shows both bands on a Southern blot. If a tumor cell loses one allele, what will its lane show?
scenes.caption: Test this on a chromosome's two copies. Suppose an enzyme cuts one copy's version, or allele, into a long piece, and the other's into a short piece. Normal tissue shows both bands on a Southern blot. If a tumor cell loses one allele, what will its lane show?
scenes.visual: Same schematic Southern membrane with size ladder on the left and two sample lanes beside it: 'Normal' and 'Tumor'. Above the normal lane, two schematic chromosome bars are cut into one long and one short fragment, producing two lit bands in the Normal lane. The Tumor lane remains blank with a bright question mark and the question text on screen.
scenes.narration: Test this on a chromosome's two copies. Suppose an enzyme cuts one copy's version, or allele, into a long piece, and the other's into a short piece. Normal tissue shows both bands on a Southern blot. If a tumor cell loses one allele, what will its lane show?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause: the question stays on screen above the schematic membrane. Normal lane holds its two glowing bands; the Tumor lane beside it pulses gently with a soft shimmer around the question mark.

scenes.tts: Only one band appears: the tumor lost one allele. Still, brightness alone can mislead, since uneven loading shifts it. A size ladder calibrates length, and a positive control shows the assay works. A loading control, like a normal-copy gene or stable-RNA reprobe, supports comparison only while brightness still tracks amount.

scenes.visual: The Tumor lane resolves to a single lit band, the missing band fading to a dashed ghost. Then the same schematic gel-membrane highlights the safeguards in turn: a glowing ladder lane and a positive-control lane; then a lower loading-control strip lighting evenly across lanes, with a small schematic gauge showing brightness tracking amount only up to a limit.

A loading control, like a normal-copy gene or stable-RNA reprobe, supports comparison only while brightness still tracks amount.

scenes.tts: In 1983, Webster Cavenee, Thaddeus Dryja and colleagues compared normal and tumor DNA in retinoblastoma. In several patients, the tumor showed only one of two chromosome thirteen alleles.
scenes.caption: In 1983, Webster Cavenee, Thaddeus Dryja and colleagues compared normal and tumor DNA in retinoblastoma. In several patients, the tumor showed only one of two chromosome 13 alleles.
scenes.visual: Same schematic Southern membrane tagged '1983 · Cavenee, Dryja et al.' (schematic): the Normal lane shows two chromosome 13 bands while the Tumor lane drops to one.
scenes.narration: In 1983, Webster Cavenee, Thaddeus Dryja and colleagues compared normal and tumor DNA in retinoblastoma. In several patients, the tumor showed only one of two chromosome 13 alleles.

scenes.tts: In 1987, Dennis Slamon and colleagues probed one hundred eighty-nine primary breast cancers. Band strength against a normal-copy control gene reported H E R two copies. About thirty percent carried extra copies; those women relapsed and died sooner, most clearly with lymph-node spread.
scenes.caption: In 1987, Dennis Slamon and colleagues probed 189 primary breast cancers. Band strength against a normal-copy control gene reported HER2 copies. About 30 percent carried extra copies; those women relapsed and died sooner, most clearly with lymph-node spread.
scenes.visual: The membrane shifts to '1987 · Slamon et al.' (schematic): each breast-tumor lane shows a HER2 band beside a steady control-gene band; the ratio of the two is drawn as a small bar under each lane, and about 30% of lanes show a HER2 band far brighter than its control.
scenes.narration: In 1987, Dennis Slamon and colleagues probed 189 primary breast cancers. Band strength against a normal-copy control gene reported HER2 copies. About 30 percent carried extra copies; those women relapsed and died sooner, most clearly with lymph-node spread.

scenes.tts: In 1996, William Kaelin and colleagues ran Northern blots on kidney-cancer cells. Some lacked the V H L gene; others had it restored. Without it, V E G F and P D G F B messenger RNA stayed high. So did G L U T one.
scenes.caption: In 1996, William Kaelin and colleagues ran Northern blots on kidney-cancer cells. Some lacked the VHL gene; others had it restored. Without it, VEGF and PDGF-B messenger RNA stayed high. So did GLUT1.
scenes.visual: Same membrane shifts to 'Northern · 1996 · Kaelin et al.' (schematic). Lanes labelled '+VHL' and '-VHL' appear; in the '-VHL' lanes the VEGF, PDGF-B and GLUT1 bands glow bright.
scenes.narration: In 1996, William Kaelin and colleagues ran Northern blots on kidney-cancer cells. Some lacked the VHL gene; others had it restored. Without it, VEGF and PDGF-B messenger RNA stayed high. So did GLUT1.

scenes.tts: That held at twenty-one and one percent oxygen. So V H L is needed for the oxygen dependence. Size sorts the smear; a probe names the sequence.
scenes.caption: That held at 21 and 1 percent oxygen. So VHL is needed for the oxygen dependence. Size sorts the smear; a probe names the sequence.
scenes.visual: Four schematic lanes compare '+VHL' and '-VHL' at 21% and 1% oxygen: '+VHL' bands change with oxygen while '-VHL' bands stay equally bright in both (schematic). On the closing sentence, the crowded smear briefly echoes behind the membrane and clears to one crisp glowing band.
scenes.narration: That held at 21 and 1 percent oxygen. So VHL is needed for the oxygen dependence. Size sorts the smear; a probe names the sequence.
